---
title: "UK Housing (London Boroughs)"
---

```{R}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
devtools::load_all()
library(tidyverse)
library(psych)
```

This chapter is inspired by Maeng et al. (2026), "High-dimensional sparsity-adaptive multiple change-point detection."

$n = 365$, $p = 32$, $q = 496$, 1995-02-01 to 2025-06-01.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Data collection"}

HM Land Registry's UK House Price Index (UKHPI) publishes monthly percentage changes in average house prices, broken out by region, from actual transaction data, at [landregistry.data.gov.uk/app/ukhpi](https://landregistry.data.gov.uk/app/ukhpi/?lang=en) — the same source the paper cites. Each of the 32 boroughs is a separate region there (e.g. `http://landregistry.data.gov.uk/id/region/camden`), and the browser serves one region at a time, so getting the full panel means 32 separate downloads, plus one more for the London aggregate.

Each download is done by hand, through the browser:

1. Open **Browse** on the UKHPI site.
2. In the location search box, type the borough name (e.g. "Camden"). It resolves under **local authority** — boroughs are not classified as a region or county there. Select it.
3. Set the date range: **From** 1995-01-01, **To** 2025-06-01.
4. Under **Type of property**, select `All property types`, `Detached houses`, `Semi-detached houses`, `Terraced houses`, and `Flats and maisonettes`.
5. Under indicators, check **Percentage change (monthly)**.
6. Click **Download**, choose **CSV**.
7. Repeat for the remaining 31 boroughs, plus once more for "London" to get the aggregate.

Excluded from the 32 boroughs: City of London — a separate financial district with its own local authority, not one of the boroughs.

This gives 33 raw files, one per region, saved unmodified to `data/real-data/uk-housing/raw/`. Each file has the full 366 monthly rows (Jan 1995 – Jun 2025) with no gaps or duplicates. The only missing value in each is `Percentage change (monthly) All property types` in the first month — there is no prior month to compute a change against.

**Variables.** For each region: `Percentage change (monthly)` for all property types and for each of detached, semi-detached, terraced, and flats/maisonettes, plus `Sales volume`.

:::

```{R uk-housing-load-data}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

raw_files <- list.files("../data/real-data/uk-housing/raw", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)

uk_housing <- raw_files |>
  map_dfr(read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(Date = as.Date(paste0(Period, "-01"), format = "%Y-%m-%d"))

X_data <- uk_housing |>
  filter(Name != "London") |>
  select(Date, Name, pct_change = `Percentage change (monthly) All property types`) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Name, values_from = pct_change) |>
  arrange(Date) |>
  drop_na()

X_mat <- as.matrix(X_data[, -1])
```

**Segmentation.** Maeng et al. detect change-points on PCA scores with BUHDA and publish no exact dates, only a figure. Running their package with their threshold selection recovers four change-points (2003-10, 2009-02, 2009-04, 2019-12) but not their fifth. Instead, we read five change-points off the plot of the series: **2003-02**, **2007-12**, **2009-01**, **2009-03** and **2019-12** (dashed vertical lines). These match the same two clusters BUHDA finds (the 2008-09 crisis and the run-up to Covid) plus one break in the early 2000s.

```{R uk-housing-segmentation-setup}
#| echo: false

cp_dates <- as.Date(c("2003-02-01", "2007-12-01", "2009-01-01", "2009-03-01", "2019-12-01"))
cp_idx   <- sapply(cp_dates, function(d) which(X_data$Date == d))
h_vec    <- rep(seq_len(length(cp_idx) + 1), diff(c(0, cp_idx, nrow(X_mat))))
h_mat    <- matrix(rep(h_vec, ncol(X_mat)), nrow(X_mat), ncol(X_mat))
seg_params <- list(h = h_mat, scenario_param = list(cp = cp_idx))

X_resid <- X_mat - segment_mean_oracle(X_mat, seg_params)
colnames(X_resid) <- colnames(X_mat)
```

## Full Resolution

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Plot

```{R uk-housing-plot-raw}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-raw
#| fig-cap: "Monthly percentage change in house prices, 32 London boroughs, 1995-2025. Dashed lines mark the 5-breakpoint segmentation."

X_data |>
  pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = "Borough", values_to = "pct_change") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Date, y = pct_change, color = Borough, group = Borough)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cp_dates, linetype = "dashed", color = "black", alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(title = "UK House Price Index, Monthly % Change (32 London Boroughs)", x = NULL, y = "Percentage change (monthly)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

```{R uk-housing-segmented-plot}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-segmented-plot
#| fig-cap: "Monthly % change, all 32 boroughs, with the 5-breakpoint segmented mean overlaid."

X_fit <- X_mat - X_resid
raw_df <- as.data.frame(X_mat) |> bind_cols(Date = X_data$Date) |> pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = "Borough", values_to = "value")
fit_df <- as.data.frame(X_fit) |> bind_cols(Date = X_data$Date) |> pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = "Borough", values_to = "value")

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = raw_df, aes(x = Date, y = value, group = Borough), color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = fit_df, aes(x = Date, y = value, group = Borough), color = "steelblue", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cp_dates, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick", alpha = 0.5) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "UK House Price % Change with segmented mean (32 boroughs)", x = NULL, y = "Percentage change (monthly)")
```

The segmented mean (blue) is flat within each of the 6 segments and jumps only at the 5 breaks (dashed red), sitting close to zero throughout since the shared shift across boroughs here is mostly higher variance, not a shared change in mean level — the gray raw series (all 32 boroughs) still carries the full month-to-month variation the segmented mean doesn't touch.

```{R uk-housing-resid-plot}

as.data.frame(X_resid) |>
  bind_cols(Date = X_data$Date) |>
  pivot_longer(-Date, names_to = "Borough", values_to = "value") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = Date, y = value, group = Borough)) +

  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Residual (monthly % change)")
```

Difference between each borough's series and its segmented mean (the blue line in the Plot tab). These residuals are what every Results tab below is computed from.

### ACF

Five randomly sampled boroughs, then the lag 1-4 autocorrelation across all 32, on the raw series.

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### ACF

```{R uk-housing-acf-sample}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-acf-sample
#| fig-cap: "Naive ACF (lags 1-4), 5 randomly sampled boroughs."
#| fig-height: 7

set.seed(1)
sample_boroughs <- sample(colnames(X_mat), 5)
par(mfrow = c(5, 1), mar = c(0, 4, 0, 1), oma = c(4, 0, 1, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
for (b in sample_boroughs) {
  acf(X_mat[, b], lag.max = 4, main = "", xaxt = "n", ylab = b)
}
axis(1)
mtext("Lag", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 2.5)
```

```{R uk-housing-acf}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-acf
#| fig-cap: "Naive autocorrelation (lags 1-4), monthly % change, 32 London boroughs."

naive_acf <- sapply(1:4, function(l) apply(X_mat, 2, function(x) acf(x, plot = FALSE, lag.max = 4)$acf[l + 1, 1, 1]))
colnames(naive_acf) <- paste0("Lag ", 1:4)
acf_df <- as.data.frame(naive_acf) |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "lag", values_to = "acf")

ggplot(acf_df, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray40") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Naive ACF")
```

Every borough has positive lag-1 autocorrelation (0.14 to 0.63, mean 0.39), with a negative dip at lag 3. This serial dependence is what makes Pearson's iid p-values anti-conservative.

#### ACF (SIP)

```{R uk-housing-sip-acf-sample}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-sip-acf-sample
#| fig-cap: "SIP-ACF (lags 1-4), same 5 boroughs."
#| fig-height: 7

par(mfrow = c(5, 1), mar = c(2, 4, 0, 1), oma = c(2, 0, 1, 0), mgp = c(1.8, 1, 0))
for (b in sample_boroughs) {
  suppressWarnings(SIP::SIP.acf(X_mat[, b], lag.max = 4, main = "", plot = TRUE))
  mtext(b, side = 2, line = 2.5, cex = 0.7)
}
mtext("Lag", side = 1, outer = TRUE, line = 0.5)
```

```{R uk-housing-sip-acf}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-sip-acf
#| fig-cap: "SIP-ACF (lags 1-4), monthly % change, 32 London boroughs."

sip_acf <- sapply(1:4, function(l) apply(X_mat, 2, function(x) suppressWarnings(SIP::SIP.acf(x, lag.max = 4, plot = FALSE)$acf[l + 1])))
colnames(sip_acf) <- paste0("Lag ", 1:4)
sip_df <- as.data.frame(sip_acf) |> pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "lag", values_to = "acf")

ggplot(sip_df, aes(x = lag, y = acf)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1), color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "SIP-ACF")
```

SIP-ACF is not usable here. 12 of 32 boroughs fall outside the valid range [-1, 1] at lag 1 (dashed lines), with a median of -0.50 and extremes near -25. Removing the five known change-points leaves this essentially unchanged, so the cause is not the mean shifts. We use the plain ACF.

:::

### Trend

```{R uk-housing-trend-helper}
#| echo: false

uk_housing_trend_terms <- function(X) {
  n <- nrow(X)
  window <- max(10, floor(n / 5))
  idx <- combn(ncol(X), 2)

  ece_terms <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
    i <- idx[1, k]; j <- idx[2, k]
    rolling_mean(lag_term(X[, i], X[, j]), window)
  })
  naive_R <- apply(X, 2, function(col) col - rolling_mean(col, window))
  naive_terms <- sapply(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
    i <- idx[1, k]; j <- idx[2, k]
    rolling_mean(naive_R[, i] * naive_R[, j], window)
  })
  list(ece = ece_terms, naive = naive_terms, window = window)
}

uk_housing_plot_trend <- function(term_mat, dates, title) {
  tibble(
    Date = dates,
    med  = apply(term_mat, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE),
    q25  = apply(term_mat, 1, quantile, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    q75  = apply(term_mat, 1, quantile, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = Date)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.3, na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_line(aes(y = med), color = "steelblue", na.rm = TRUE) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray40", linetype = "dashed") +
    theme_minimal() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Rolling-mean term (covariance scale)", title = title)
}

trend_terms <- uk_housing_trend_terms(X_resid)
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### Naive

```{R uk-housing-trend-naive}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-trend-naive
#| fig-cap: "Naive covariance term, median and IQR across 496 borough pairs, rolling window = 73 months."

uk_housing_plot_trend(trend_terms$naive, X_data$Date, "Naive covariance term (median +/- IQR, 496 pairs)")
```

#### Mean-Shift-Invariant

```{R uk-housing-trend-ece}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-trend-ece
#| fig-cap: "ECE (lag-1 difference) covariance term, median and IQR across 496 borough pairs, rolling window = 73 months."

uk_housing_plot_trend(trend_terms$ece, X_data$Date, "ECE covariance term (median +/- IQR, 496 pairs)")
```

:::

Each curve is built from the rolling mean of the covariance term for every borough pair (496 time series). At each time point, the line is the median across pairs and the band is the interquartile range.

### Kappa

The default `ece_pval()` z-test (`kappa = "gaussian"`) assumes the fourth-moment terms take their Gaussian values (`k40 = k04 = 3`, `k22 = 1 + 2ρ²`, `k31 = k13 = 3ρ`). We check that assumption across all `choose(32, 2)` = 496 borough pairs, estimating these terms directly (`ece.kappa(..., method = "mom")`) instead of assuming them:

```{R uk-housing-kappa}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-kappa
#| fig-cap: "Kappa terms across 496 borough pairs, monthly % change. Dashed line marks the Gaussian reference."
#| fig-height: 3.5

idx <- combn(ncol(X_mat), 2)
kap <- purrr::map_dfr(seq_len(ncol(idx)), function(k) {
  i <- idx[1, k]
  j <- idx[2, k]
  r <- ece.kappa(X_mat[, i], X_mat[, j], method = "mom")
  tibble(k40 = r$k40, k31 = r$k31, k22 = r$k22, k13 = r$k13, k04 = r$k04)
})
kap_long <- kap |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "term", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(term = factor(term, levels = c("k40", "k31", "k22", "k13", "k04")))
kappa_ref <- tibble(
  term     = factor(c("k40", "k31", "k22", "k13", "k04"), levels = c("k40", "k31", "k22", "k13", "k04")),
  gaussian = c(3, 0, 1, 0, 3)
)

ggplot(kap_long, aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(data = kappa_ref, aes(xintercept = gaussian), color = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~term, scales = "free", ncol = 5) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Count", title = "Kappa terms across 496 borough pairs (dashed = Gaussian reference)")
```

`k40` and `k04` cluster a bit above the Gaussian reference of 3 (median 4.3 and 3.6) with a long right tail out past 20 — heavier-tailed marginals than Gaussian, the same direction `cpi-components.qmd` found for `Apparel` and `Transportation`. `k22` centers near 1, close to its small-ρ Gaussian reference, and `k31`/`k13` center near 0 as expected for mostly-small correlations. The fat tails in `k40`/`k04` mean the default `kappa = "gaussian"` z-test — what `ece_pval()` assumes — understates the true standard error for at least some pairs, so the Results section below uses the null-restricted z-test instead (`kappa = ece.kappa(X, rho = 0, method = "mom")`, `rho = 0`), which only needs `k22` rather than all five Gaussian values to hold — the same fix `cpi-components.qmd` applies for the same reason. Neither this Kappa check nor the ACF check above touches the sign-flip question directly — a heavier-tailed marginal or serial correlation changes a pair's standard error and p-value, not the sign of its point estimate — so a flipped sign in the ECE heatmap below is more likely a real trend-removal effect than a kappa or autocorrelation artifact.

### Size

To check whether the global tests hold their size on this panel, we break the cross-borough dependence while keeping each series' own dynamics: every column of `X_resid` is circularly shifted by an independent random offset, so the null of a diagonal correlation matrix is true by construction. We rerun the tests on 200 shifted copies. A valid test gives uniform p-values (density 1 in every bin).

```{R uk-size-sim}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false

size_file <- "../data/real-data/uk-housing/size-sim.rds"

if (file.exists(size_file)) {
  size_sim <- readRDS(size_file)
} else {
  shift_cols <- function(X) {
    n <- nrow(X)
    apply(X, 2, function(x) x[((seq_len(n) + sample(n, 1)) %% n) + 1])
  }

  set.seed(123)
  size_sim <- map_dfr(1:200, function(b) {
    Xs <- shift_cols(X_resid)
    tibble(
      rep = b,
      `Bootstrap Multiplier` = ece.test(Xs, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value,
      `Parametric Bootstrap` = ece.test(Xs, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value,
      `Parametric Bootstrap (PSD, Centered + Normalized)` =
        bs_parametric_test(Xs, force_psd = TRUE, center = TRUE, normalize = TRUE)$p.value
    )
  })

  dir.create(dirname(size_file), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
  saveRDS(size_sim, size_file)
}

size_long <- size_sim |>
  pivot_longer(-rep, names_to = "Method", values_to = "p") |>
  mutate(Method = factor(Method, levels = names(size_sim)[-1]))
```

```{R uk-size-hist}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-size-hist
#| fig-cap: "P-values of each global test on 200 independently shifted copies of the segmented residuals. A valid test has density 1 in every bin."
#| fig-height: 3

ggplot(size_long, aes(x = p)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), breaks = seq(0, 1, by = 0.1), fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~Method, ncol = 3, labeller = label_wrap_gen(24)) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "p-value", y = "Density")
```

:::

With those two caveats in hand — Pearson's p-values run anti-conservative under positive autocorrelation, and ECE's default Gaussian kappa understates the standard error for heavy-tailed pairs — the pairwise correlation matrix is easier to read as a heatmap than a table.

```{R uk-housing-cor-heatmap-helper}
#| echo: false

uk_housing_plot_cor_heatmap <- function(cor_mat, pval_mat, fill_lab, blank_diag = FALSE) {
  cor_df <- as.data.frame(cor_mat) |>
    rownames_to_column("Borough1") |>
    pivot_longer(-Borough1, names_to = "Borough2", values_to = "correlation")
  pval_df <- as.data.frame(pval_mat) |>
    rownames_to_column("Borough1") |>
    pivot_longer(-Borough1, names_to = "Borough2", values_to = "p_value")
  df <- left_join(cor_df, pval_df, by = c("Borough1", "Borough2"))
  # Covariance heatmaps: the diagonal holds variances, which would swamp the
  # off-diagonal color scale, so show it as gray NA instead.
  if (blank_diag) df$correlation[df$Borough1 == df$Borough2] <- NA
  bound <- max(abs(df$correlation), na.rm = TRUE)
  sig_df <- df |> filter(Borough1 != Borough2, p_value < 0.05)

  ggplot(df, aes(x = Borough1, y = Borough2, fill = correlation)) +
    geom_tile() +
    geom_text(data = sig_df, aes(label = "*"), color = "black", size = 3, vjust = 0.75) +
    scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick", midpoint = 0, limits = c(-bound, bound), na.value = "firebrick") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, size = 6), axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6)) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = fill_lab)
}

# Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment on the 496 unique off-diagonal p-values (each
# pair appears twice in a symmetric p-value matrix; adjusting the full
# vectorized matrix would double-count every test and treat the zeroed
# diagonal as 32 more tests).
bh_adjust_pmat <- function(pmat) {
  p   <- ncol(pmat)
  idx <- combn(p, 2)
  q   <- p.adjust(pmat[cbind(idx[1, ], idx[2, ])], method = "BH")
  qmat <- matrix(NA_real_, p, p, dimnames = dimnames(pmat))
  qmat[cbind(idx[1, ], idx[2, ])] <- q
  qmat[cbind(idx[2, ], idx[1, ])] <- q
  diag(qmat) <- 0
  qmat
}

# Null-restricted z-test (rho = 0): avoids assuming the Gaussian k40/k04/k31/k13
# values, which the Kappa diagnostic tab above shows are misspecified for this
# data. Only k22 needs estimating, since every other kappa term carries a
# factor of rho or rho^2 and drops out algebraically at rho = 0.
ece_pval_null <- function(X) {
  p <- ncol(X)
  pval_mat <- matrix(NA, p, p)
  colnames(pval_mat) <- rownames(pval_mat) <- colnames(X)
  for (i in 1:(p - 1)) {
    for (j in (i + 1):p) {
      pair <- cbind(X[, i], X[, j])
      pval <- ece.test(pair, type = "z.test", kappa = ece.kappa(pair, rho = 0, method = "mom"), rho = 0)$p.value
      pval_mat[i, j] <- pval
      pval_mat[j, i] <- pval
    }
  }
  diag(pval_mat) <- 0
  pval_mat
}
```

## Results

All Results below use `X_resid` — residuals after removing the 5-breakpoint segmented mean established above — rather than the raw panel. The Full Resolution ACF tab already showed this segmentation doesn't touch the panel's real driver (ongoing month-to-month serial correlation), so the segmented and raw versions of these results were close throughout; segmented is kept as the single, primary version rather than showing both.

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Pearson

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### p < 0.05

```{R uk-housing-cor-heatmap}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-cor-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise Pearson correlation on residuals after removing the 5-breakpoint segmented mean."
#| fig-height: 7

cor_mat      <- cor(X_resid, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
pearson_pmat <- cor_pval(X_resid)
dimnames(pearson_pmat) <- list(colnames(X_resid), colnames(X_resid))
uk_housing_plot_cor_heatmap(cor_mat, pearson_pmat, "Pearson r")
```

#### BH q < 0.05

```{R uk-housing-cor-heatmap-bh}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-cor-heatmap-bh
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise Pearson correlation on residuals after removing the 5-breakpoint segmented mean (BH-adjusted)."
#| fig-height: 7

pearson_qmat <- bh_adjust_pmat(pearson_pmat)
uk_housing_plot_cor_heatmap(cor_mat, pearson_qmat, "Pearson r")
```

### Diagonal z-test

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### p < 0.05

```{R uk-housing-diag-heatmap}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-diag-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise ECE covariance on residuals, with significance from the diagonal z-test."
#| fig-height: 7

diag_pmat <- matrix(NA_real_, ncol(X_resid), ncol(X_resid), dimnames = list(colnames(X_resid), colnames(X_resid)))
for (k in seq_len(ncol(combn(ncol(X_resid), 2)))) {
  ij <- combn(ncol(X_resid), 2)[, k]
  diag_pmat[ij[1], ij[2]] <- diag_pmat[ij[2], ij[1]] <-
    suppressWarnings(ece.test(X_resid[, ij], type = "z.test.hac.center")$p.value)
}
diag(diag_pmat) <- 0

ece_cov_mat <- ece.cov(X_resid)
dimnames(ece_cov_mat) <- list(colnames(X_resid), colnames(X_resid))
uk_housing_plot_cor_heatmap(ece_cov_mat, diag_pmat, "ECE cov", blank_diag = TRUE)
```

#### BH q < 0.05

```{R uk-housing-diag-heatmap-bh}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-diag-heatmap-bh
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise ECE covariance on residuals, with significance from the diagonal z-test (BH-adjusted)."
#| fig-height: 7

diag_qmat <- bh_adjust_pmat(diag_pmat)
uk_housing_plot_cor_heatmap(ece_cov_mat, diag_qmat, "ECE cov", blank_diag = TRUE)
```

:::

The null-restricted z-test above estimates the standard error from `k22` under the null. The diagonal z-test (`z.test.hac.center`) instead uses the variance of the ECE terms themselves, with no kappa assumption. The terms are demeaned before the variance is estimated, so the variance is not inflated when the true correlation is nonzero. The test is a test of the ECE covariance $\hat\sigma_{xy} = \bar S$, so the heatmaps above show that same covariance as the fill (in squared percentage-point units) and take the stars from the diagonal z-test. Fill and stars are on the same scale, but the tiles are no longer on the correlation scale of the ECE tab, so colors are not comparable across the two. The diagonal (the variances) is shown in the top color (red) so it does not set the color scale.

### Diagonal

The 496 pairwise tests above run into the multiple-testing problem directly: at α = 0.05, roughly 50 false positives are expected across 992 off-diagonal entries by chance alone. A joint test of a single null hypothesis — the full 32x32 correlation matrix (of segmented residuals) is diagonal, i.e. no borough pair is correlated — sidesteps that problem entirely, at the cost of not saying which pairs.

```{R uk-housing-diagonal-tests}
#| echo: false

set.seed(123)
bs_mult_p  <- ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.multiplier")$p.value
set.seed(123)
bs_param_p <- ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.lag1.diag.psd")$p.value
set.seed(123)
bs_psd_p <- ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.psd")$p.value
set.seed(123)
bs_psd_center_p <- ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.psd.center")$p.value
set.seed(123)
bs_psd_norm_p <- ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.psd.norm")$p.value
set.seed(123)
bs_psd_cn_p <- bs_parametric_test(X_resid, force_psd = TRUE, center = TRUE, normalize = TRUE)$p.value
set.seed(123)
bs_naive_p <- ece.test(X_resid, type = "bs.parametric.naive")$p.value
bartlett_p <- cortest.bartlett(cor(X_resid), nrow(X_resid))$p.value

diag_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c(
    "Bootstrap Multiplier",
    "Parametric Bootstrap",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (PSD)",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (PSD, Centered)",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (PSD, Normalized)",
    "Parametric Bootstrap (PSD, Centered + Normalized)"
  ),
  `p-value` = round(c(bs_mult_p, bs_param_p, bs_psd_p, bs_psd_center_p, bs_psd_norm_p, bs_psd_cn_p), 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(diag_results, caption = "Joint test of H0: the 32x32 correlation matrix of segmented-mean residuals is diagonal.")
```

```{R uk-housing-diagonal-tests-naive}
#| echo: false

naive_results <- data.frame(
  Method = c("Parametric Bootstrap (Naive)", "Bartlett Test"),
  `p-value` = round(c(bs_naive_p, bartlett_p), 3),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(naive_results, caption = "Naive tests of the same hypothesis.")
```

:::

## Why the Diagonal and Delta-Method Tests Disagree

```{R uk-housing-diag-vs-delta-z}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-diag-vs-delta-z
#| fig-cap: "Absolute z-statistic of the diagonal test against that of the null-restricted delta-method test, one point per borough pair. Dashed line: equal statistics; dotted lines: 1.96."
#| fig-height: 4.5

pair_idx <- combn(ncol(X_resid), 2)
pair_ij  <- cbind(pair_idx[1, ], pair_idx[2, ])

z_df <- tibble(
  z_delta = qnorm(ece_pmat[pair_ij] / 2, lower.tail = FALSE),
  z_diag  = qnorm(diag_pmat[pair_ij] / 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
)

ggplot(z_df, aes(x = z_delta, y = z_diag)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1.96, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1.96, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  coord_equal() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "|z| (delta method)", y = "|z| (diagonal)",
       title = sprintf("z-statistics, %d borough pairs", nrow(pair_ij)))
```

```{R uk-housing-diag-vs-delta-se}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-diag-vs-delta-se
#| fig-cap: "Ratio of the diagonal (centered) SE to the null-restricted delta-method SE, both on the correlation scale, against the absolute ECE correlation."
#| fig-height: 4

pair_idx <- combn(ncol(X_resid), 2)
pair_ij  <- cbind(pair_idx[1, ], pair_idx[2, ])

se_df <- map_dfr(seq_len(nrow(pair_ij)), \(k) {
  pair <- X_resid[, pair_ij[k, ]]
  sc <- sqrt(ece.cov(pair[, 1]) * ece.cov(pair[, 2]))
  tibble(
    rho = abs(ece_cor[pair_ij[k, 1], pair_ij[k, 2]]),
    se_diag  = z_test_hac(pair, center = TRUE)$se / sc,
    se_delta = ece.cor.se(pair[, 1], pair[, 2], kappa = ece.kappa(pair, rho = 0, method = "mom"), rho = 0)
  )
})

ggplot(se_df, aes(x = rho, y = se_diag / se_delta)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "steelblue") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "|ECE correlation|", y = "SE (diagonal) / SE (delta method)",
       title = "SE ratio, 496 borough pairs")
```

## Downsampling

The Diagnostics ACF tab shows strong positive serial correlation at lag 1. Keeping every other month removes half the data, and lag $j$ of the downsampled series is lag $2j$ of the original. We segment first and then downsample the residuals `X_resid`, since the two breaks at 2009-01 and 2009-03 are only two months apart. As in `gnss.qmd`, each subsample starts at the first month and takes every k-th one (`seq(1, n, by = k)`).

```{R uk-housing-down-acf}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-uk-housing-down-acf
#| fig-cap: "Downsampling by k = 2 (every other month) and k = 3 (every third month), starting at the first month. Fraction of the 32 boroughs whose ACF falls outside the 95% band (±1.96/sqrt(n)) at each lag of the downsampled series. Dashed line: 5% expected under no dependence."
#| fig-height: 3.5

down_lags <- 10

down_frac <- map_dfr(2:3, function(k) {
  Xd <- X_resid[seq(1, nrow(X_resid), by = k), ]
  band <- 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(Xd))
  acf_d <- sapply(seq_len(down_lags), function(l)
    apply(Xd, 2, function(x) acf(x, plot = FALSE, lag.max = down_lags)$acf[l + 1]))
  tibble(k = paste0("k = ", k, " (n = ", nrow(Xd), ")"),
         lag = seq_len(down_lags), frac = colMeans(abs(acf_d) > band))
})

ggplot(down_frac, aes(x = factor(lag), y = frac)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  facet_wrap(~k, ncol = 1) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(x = "Lag (downsampled series)", y = "Fraction outside band")
```
